title: The Aesop for Children
sourceTitle: The Aesop for Children, with Pictures by Milo Winter
author: Aesop (illustrated by Milo Winter)
licenseEvidence: Gutenberg #19994: public domain in the USA; first published by Rand McNally & Co., 1919
description: The classic 1919 Aesop collection with Milo Winter's beloved pictures: 147 short fables, each ending in a moral. Read three fables aloud, let your child tell them back, and copy one moral as handwriting practice. The full illustrated text is free online.
includes: One question per fable with a kid-friendly answer
Link to the free illustrated text for every fable

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The Wolf and the Kid, The Tortoise and the Ducks, The Young Crab and His Mother
steps: Read aloud: The Wolf and the Kid, The Tortoise and the Ducks, The Young Crab and His Mother
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Wolf and the Kid" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening

links.label: Read “The Young Crab and His Mother”

questions: Why was the Wolf sorry he played music for the Kid?
Why did the Tortoise fall when the Ducks carried him?
What was wrong with the Mother Crab's advice?
answers: He forgot what he came to do. Don't let anything distract you from what you set out to do.
He opened his mouth to show off. Showing off and being nosy can get you hurt.
She couldn't walk straight herself. Show a good example before you tell others what to do.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The Frogs and the Ox, The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox, Belling the Cat
steps: Read aloud: The Frogs and the Ox, The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox, Belling the Cat
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox" in your best handwriting
Act out one fable with toys or puppets

links.label: Read “The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox”

questions: What happened when the old Frog tried to puff up as big as the Ox?
How did the Cock trick the Fox who wanted to eat him?
Why did no Mouse want to put the bell on the Cat?
answers: She burst. Don't try to do something that can't be done.
He sent the Fox around the tree to his friend the Dog. If you try to trick others, you may get tricked back.
It was too dangerous. Saying something should be done is easier than doing it.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The Eagle and the Jackdaw, The Boy and the Filberts, Hercules and the Wagoner
steps: Read aloud: The Eagle and the Jackdaw, The Boy and the Filberts, Hercules and the Wagoner
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "Hercules and the Wagoner" from dictation, then check it against the book
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today
questions: Why couldn't the Jackdaw carry off a ram like the Eagle?
How could the Boy get his hand out of the pitcher?
What did Hercules tell the Farmer to do?
answers: He wasn't strong enough and got stuck. Don't think you can do more than you really can.
Let go of some nuts. Don't try to take too much at once.
Push the wheel himself. Try your best first, then you'll get help.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The Kid and the Wolf, The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse, The Fox and the Grapes
steps: Read aloud: The Kid and the Wolf, The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse, The Fox and the Grapes
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Kid and the Wolf" and underline the most important word
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life

links.label: Read “The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse”

questions: Why could the Kid be rude to the Wolf from the roof?
Why did the Town Mouse's friend go home to the country?
Why did the Fox say the grapes were sour?
answers: He was safe up high. Don't say mean things just because you feel safe.
The town was full of danger. A safe, simple life is better than fancy food and fear.
He couldn't reach them. People sometimes pretend they don't want what they can't get.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The Bundle of Sticks, The Wolf and the Crane, The Ass and His Driver
steps: Read aloud: The Bundle of Sticks, The Wolf and the Crane, The Ass and His Driver
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Wolf and the Crane" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
questions: Why couldn't the sons break the bundle of sticks?
What "reward" did the Crane get for helping the Wolf?
What happened when the Ass wouldn't listen to his driver?
answers: The sticks were held together. We are strong when we stick together.
Only her life. Don't expect thanks from someone mean.
He fell off the cliff. Listen to good advice from people who know better.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: The Oxen and the Wheels, The Lion and the Mouse, The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf
steps: Read aloud: The Oxen and the Wheels, The Lion and the Mouse, The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf" in your best handwriting
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening

links.label: Read “The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf”

questions: Who were working hardest, the Oxen or the creaking Wheels?
How did the little Mouse help the Lion?
Why didn't the villagers come when the Boy really saw a wolf?
answers: The Oxen. The ones who complain the most often have it easiest.
She chewed the net and set him free. Being kind is never wasted, even small friends can help.
He had lied too many times. People won't believe a liar even when he tells the truth.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: The Gnat and the Bull, The Plane Tree, The Farmer and the Stork
steps: Read aloud: The Gnat and the Bull, The Plane Tree, The Farmer and the Stork
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Gnat and the Bull" from dictation, then check it against the book
Act out one fable with toys or puppets
questions: Did the Bull even notice the Gnat on his horn?
What did the travelers call the tree that gave them shade?
Why did the Farmer punish the Stork too?
answers: No. Some think they are very important when others hardly notice them.
Useless. People often forget to be thankful for the good things they have.
He was caught with the thieving Cranes. People judge you by the friends you are with.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: The Sheep and the Pig, The Travelers and the Purse, The Lion and the Ass
steps: Read aloud: The Sheep and the Pig, The Travelers and the Purse, The Lion and the Ass
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Travelers and the Purse" and underline the most important word
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today
questions: Why did the Pig squeal so much more than the Sheep?
Why wouldn't the man share the trouble with his friend?
What did the Lion do when the Ass made fun of him?
answers: The Sheep would only lose wool but the Pig would be eaten. It's easy to be brave when nothing bad will happen to you.
He wouldn't share the purse. If you won't share the good things, don't expect help with the bad.
He ignored him and walked on. Don't let a silly person's words bother you.

lessons.title: Lesson 9: The Frogs Who Wished for a King, The Owl and the Grasshopper, The Wolf and His Shadow
steps: Read aloud: The Frogs Who Wished for a King, The Owl and the Grasshopper, The Wolf and His Shadow
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Wolf and His Shadow" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life

links.label: Read “The Frogs Who Wished for a King”

questions: Were the Frogs happy with the king they asked for?
How did the Owl catch the Grasshopper?
Why was the Wolf caught by the Lion?
answers: No, the Stork ate them. Make sure a change will really be better before you ask for it.
She praised his singing and offered him a treat. Watch out when an enemy says nice things.
He thought he was as big as his shadow. Don't let pretending make you forget what's real.

lessons.title: Lesson 10: The Oak and the Reeds, The Rat and the Elephant, The Boys and the Frogs
steps: Read aloud: The Oak and the Reeds, The Rat and the Elephant, The Boys and the Frogs
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Oak and the Reeds" in your best handwriting
questions: Why did the Reeds survive the storm but the Oak fell?
What did the Cat show the proud Rat?
What did the Frog tell the Boys throwing stones?
answers: The Reeds bent with the wind. Sometimes it's wiser to bend than to be stubborn.
He was not as important as the Elephant. Being a little like someone great doesn't make you great.
Your fun means death to us. Think about whether your fun hurts someone else.

lessons.title: Lesson 11: The Crow and the Pitcher, The Ants and the Grasshopper, The Ass Carrying the Image
steps: Read aloud: The Crow and the Pitcher, The Ants and the Grasshopper, The Ass Carrying the Image
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Ants and the Grasshopper" from dictation, then check it against the book
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening
questions: How did the Crow get a drink from the pitcher?
Why did the Ants refuse to feed the Grasshopper?
Who were the people really bowing to?
answers: He dropped in pebbles until the water rose. When you're stuck, think hard and you may find a way.
He played all summer instead of working. There is a time to work and a time to play.
The image, not the Ass. Don't take credit for what belongs to someone else.

lessons.title: Lesson 12: A Raven and a Swan, The Two Goats, The Ass and the Load of Salt
steps: Read aloud: A Raven and a Swan, The Two Goats, The Ass and the Load of Salt
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Ass and the Load of Salt" and underline the most important word
Act out one fable with toys or puppets

links.label: Read “The Ass and the Load of Salt”

questions: Did the Raven turn white by living like a Swan?
Why did both Goats fall into the river?
Why did the Ass's trick fail the second time?
answers: No, he just got thin. Changing what you do won't change who you are.
Neither would let the other pass. Being stubborn can hurt everyone, so sometimes give way.
He carried sponges, not salt, so the load got heavier. A trick that worked once won't work every time.

lessons.title: Lesson 13: The Lion and the Gnat, The Leap at Rhodes, The Cock and the Jewel
steps: Read aloud: The Lion and the Gnat, The Leap at Rhodes, The Cock and the Jewel
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Lion and the Gnat" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today
questions: What happened to the Gnat after he beat the Lion?
How did the hearers answer the man who bragged about his big jump?
Why did the Cock not want the jewel?
answers: A spider caught him. Don't get so proud of winning that you stop being careful.
Jump it here and now. What you do counts more than what you brag about.
He couldn't eat it. Something precious means nothing to someone who doesn't care about it.

lessons.title: Lesson 14: The Monkey and the Camel, The Wild Boar and the Fox, The Ass, the Fox, and the Lion
steps: Read aloud: The Monkey and the Camel, The Wild Boar and the Fox, The Ass, the Fox, and the Lion
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Wild Boar and the Fox" in your best handwriting
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life

links.label: Read “The Wild Boar and the Fox”
Read “The Ass, the Fox, and the Lion”

questions: Why was the Camel chased away?
Why did the Boar sharpen his tusks with no enemy around?
What happened to the Fox after he betrayed the Ass?
answers: He tried to dance like the Monkey and looked silly. Don't copy others just to show off.
There'd be no time when danger came. Get ready before trouble comes.
The Lion ate him too. If you betray a friend, you may be betrayed.

lessons.title: Lesson 15: The Birds, the Beasts, and the Bat, The Lion, the Bear, and the Fox, The Wolf and the Lamb
steps: Read aloud: The Birds, the Beasts, and the Bat, The Lion, the Bear, and the Fox, The Wolf and the Lamb
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Wolf and the Lamb" from dictation, then check it against the book

links.label: Read “The Birds, the Beasts, and the Bat”
Read “The Lion, the Bear, and the Fox”

questions: Why did the Bat end up with no friends?
Who got the kid that the Lion and Bear fought over?
Why did the Wolf eat the Lamb even though she did nothing wrong?
answers: He kept switching sides. People who trick others end up alone.
The Fox. Sometimes those who do the work don't get the reward.
He wanted to and made up excuses. A bully won't listen to what's fair.

lessons.title: Lesson 16: The Wolf and the Sheep, The Hares and the Frogs, The Fox and the Stork
steps: Read aloud: The Wolf and the Sheep, The Hares and the Frogs, The Fox and the Stork
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Wolf and the Sheep" and underline the most important word
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening
questions: Why wouldn't the Sheep bring the Wolf a drink?
What made the Hares stop being so scared?
How did the Stork pay the Fox back?
answers: She knew he would eat her. It's easy to see through a sneaky person.
They saw Frogs afraid of them. Someone always has it worse than you.
She served food in a tall jar he couldn't reach. Don't play a trick you wouldn't want played on you.

lessons.title: Lesson 17: The Travelers and the Sea, The Wolf and the Lion, The Stag and His Reflection
steps: Read aloud: The Travelers and the Sea, The Wolf and the Lion, The Stag and His Reflection
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Wolf and the Lion" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Act out one fable with toys or puppets
questions: What did the travelers find when the "ship" came in?
Why couldn't the Wolf complain when the Lion took his lamb?
What did the Stag think of his legs and his antlers?
answers: Only some sticks of wood. Don't let wishing make you forget what's real.
He stole it first. Something taken wrongly can be lost the same way.
He hated his legs and loved his antlers, but his legs saved him and his antlers trapped him. Useful things matter more than pretty things.

lessons.title: Lesson 18: The Peacock, The Mice and the Weasels, The Wolf and the Lean Dog
steps: Read aloud: The Peacock, The Mice and the Weasels, The Wolf and the Lean Dog
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Wolf and the Lean Dog" in your best handwriting
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today

links.label: Read “The Wolf and the Lean Dog”

questions: Why did the Peacock's beautiful tail make him unhappy?
Why were the Mouse leaders caught?
Why did the Wolf go away hungry from the lean Dog?
answers: It was too heavy to fly. Don't give up being free just for looking fancy.
Their fancy headdresses wouldn't fit in the holes. Being important can come with dangers.
He believed the Dog's promise to get fat first. Don't trust promises from someone who wants to fool you.

lessons.title: Lesson 19: The Fox and the Lion, The Lion and the Ass, The Dog and His Master's Dinner
steps: Read aloud: The Fox and the Lion, The Lion and the Ass, The Dog and His Master's Dinner
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Fox and the Lion" from dictation, then check it against the book
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life

links.label: Read “The Dog and His Master's Dinner”

questions: Why did the Fox stop being afraid of the Lion?
Why wasn't the Lion scared of the braying Ass?
Why did the Dog finally eat his master's dinner?
answers: He saw him many times. Getting used to something dangerous can make you forget it's dangerous.
He knew the Ass was all noise. A loud bragger doesn't scare those who know him.
He stopped to argue with the other dogs. Don't stop to argue with temptation, just walk away.

lessons.title: Lesson 20: The Vain Jackdaw and His Borrowed Feathers, The Monkey and the Dolphin, The Wolf and the Ass
steps: Read aloud: The Vain Jackdaw and His Borrowed Feathers, The Monkey and the Dolphin, The Wolf and the Ass
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Monkey and the Dolphin" and underline the most important word

links.label: Read “The Vain Jackdaw and His Borrowed Feathers”

questions: What happened when the Jackdaw wore peacock feathers?
Why did the Dolphin leave the Monkey?
How did the Ass escape the Wolf?
answers: The Peacocks pulled them off and his own flock chased him. Wearing borrowed things doesn't make you better.
The Monkey kept telling lies. One lie leads to another lie.
He tricked him into looking at his hoof and kicked him. Stick to what you are good at.

lessons.title: Lesson 21: The Monkey and the Cat, The Dogs and the Fox, The Dogs and the Hides
steps: Read aloud: The Monkey and the Cat, The Dogs and the Fox, The Dogs and the Hides
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Dogs and the Hides" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening
questions: Who ate the chestnuts the Cat pulled from the fire?
Why did the Fox laugh at the Dogs tearing the lion skin?
Why did the Dogs burst?
answers: The Monkey. A flatterer says nice things to get something from you.
They wouldn't dare if the Lion were alive. It's mean and easy to pick on someone who can't fight back.
They tried to drink the whole stream. Don't try to do impossible things.

lessons.title: Lesson 22: The Rabbit, the Weasel, and the Cat, The Bear and the Bees, The Fox and the Leopard
steps: Read aloud: The Rabbit, the Weasel, and the Cat, The Bear and the Bees, The Fox and the Leopard
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Rabbit, the Weasel, and the Cat" in your best handwriting
Act out one fable with toys or puppets

links.label: Read “The Rabbit, the Weasel, and the Cat”

questions: Who won when the Rabbit and Weasel asked the Cat to judge?
Why did the Bear end up hiding in a pool?
What did the Fox say was real beauty?
answers: The Cat, she grabbed them both. Be careful asking a strong bully to settle your fight.
He got angry at one bee and the whole swarm came. It's better to put up with a small hurt than to make it worse by getting mad.
A clever mind, not a spotted coat. Looking fine outside doesn't mean you're clever inside.

lessons.title: Lesson 23: The Heron, The Cock and the Fox, The Dog in the Manger
steps: Read aloud: The Heron, The Cock and the Fox, The Dog in the Manger
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Cock and the Fox" from dictation, then check it against the book
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today
questions: What did the Heron end up eating?
How did the Cock trick the Fox?
Why did the Dog keep the hay from the Cattle?
answers: A tiny Snail. If you are too picky, you may end up with little or nothing.
He said dogs were coming. A trickster can be tricked too.
He was being mean, even though he couldn't eat it. Don't keep things from others that you can't use yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 24: The Wolf and the Goat, The Ass and the Grasshoppers, The Mule
steps: Read aloud: The Wolf and the Goat, The Ass and the Grasshoppers, The Mule
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Mule" and underline the most important word
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life
questions: Why didn't the Goat come down for the Wolf's grass?
What happened to the Ass who ate only dew?
What did the Mule remember when he got tired?
answers: She knew he wanted to eat her. Don't trust an invitation from someone who's only thinking of himself.
He starved. You can't change how nature works.
His father was a donkey. Don't brag about your family unless you're sure.

lessons.title: Lesson 25: The Fox and the Goat, The Cat, the Cock, and the Young Mouse, The Wolf and the Shepherd
steps: Read aloud: The Fox and the Goat, The Cat, the Cock, and the Young Mouse, The Wolf and the Shepherd
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Fox and the Goat" (younger children can trace it after you write it)

links.label: Read “The Cat, the Cock, and the Young Mouse”

questions: Why did the Goat end up stuck in the well?
Which animal was really dangerous to the young Mouse?
What happened when the Shepherd trusted the Wolf to guard the sheep?
answers: He jumped in without thinking. Look before you leap.
The quiet Cat, not the noisy Cock. Don't judge by how things look.
The Wolf ate them. A wolf is always a wolf.

lessons.title: Lesson 26: The Peacock and the Crane, The Farmer and the Cranes, The Farmer and His Sons
steps: Read aloud: The Peacock and the Crane, The Farmer and the Cranes, The Farmer and His Sons
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Farmer and the Cranes" in your best handwriting
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening
questions: How was the Crane better than the Peacock?
When did the Cranes really leave the field?
What treasure did the sons find in the vineyard?
answers: He could fly high. Being useful matters more than looking pretty.
When the Farmer used real stones, not just pretend. Big talk doesn't mean someone can't really act.
A big harvest from digging. Hard work is a treasure itself.

lessons.title: Lesson 27: The Two Pots, The Goose and the Golden Egg, The Fighting Bulls and the Frog
steps: Read aloud: The Two Pots, The Goose and the Golden Egg, The Fighting Bulls and the Frog
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Fighting Bulls and the Frog" from dictation, then check it against the book
Act out one fable with toys or puppets

links.label: Read “The Goose and the Golden Egg”
Read “The Fighting Bulls and the Frog”

questions: What happened when the brass and clay pots traveled together?
Why did the Countryman lose all his gold?
Why were the Frogs afraid of the bulls fighting?
answers: The clay pot broke. Friends who are alike get along best.
He killed the goose to get all the eggs at once. Being greedy can make you lose everything.
The loser would run into the marsh and crush them. When big ones fight, little ones get hurt.

lessons.title: Lesson 28: The Mouse and the Weasel, The Farmer and the Snake, The Sick Stag
steps: Read aloud: The Mouse and the Weasel, The Farmer and the Snake, The Sick Stag
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Mouse and the Weasel" and underline the most important word
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today
questions: Why couldn't the Mouse get out of the basket?
What did the frozen Snake do after the Farmer warmed him?
Why did the Stag starve?
answers: He ate too much and got fat. Being greedy gets you into trouble.
He bit the Farmer. Don't trust someone who is wicked, even when you feel sorry for them.
His visitors ate all his food. Being a good friend means doing good, not just saying nice things.

lessons.title: Lesson 29: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats, The Spendthrift and the Swallow, The Cat and the Birds
steps: Read aloud: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats, The Spendthrift and the Swallow, The Cat and the Birds
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Spendthrift and the Swallow" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life

links.label: Read “The Goatherd and the Wild Goats”

questions: Why did the Wild Goats run away from the Goatherd?
Why did the young man sell his cloak?
Why didn't the Birds let the Cat "doctor" in?
answers: He treated his own goats badly. Don't treat old friends badly to please new ones.
He saw one swallow and thought it was summer. One sign doesn't mean something has really happened.
They knew he wanted to eat them. Don't trust someone who is only pretending to help.

lessons.title: Lesson 30: The Dog and the Oyster, The Astrologer, Three Bullocks and a Lion
steps: Read aloud: The Dog and the Oyster, The Astrologer, Three Bullocks and a Lion
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "Three Bullocks and a Lion" in your best handwriting
questions: What happened when the Dog swallowed the oyster?
Why did the Astrologer fall into the ditch?
How did the Lion finally catch the Bullocks?
answers: It hurt his tummy. If you rush, you'll be sorry later.
He was looking at the stars, not where he walked. Pay attention to little things right in front of you.
He made them quarrel and split up. We are strong when we stay together.

lessons.title: Lesson 31: Mercury and the Woodman, The Frog and the Mouse, The Fox and the Crab
steps: Read aloud: Mercury and the Woodman, The Frog and the Mouse, The Fox and the Crab
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "Mercury and the Woodman" from dictation, then check it against the book
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening
questions: What did Mercury give the honest Woodman?
What happened to the Frog who tied the Mouse to him?
What happened when the Crab left the seashore?
answers: All three axes. Telling the truth is always best.
A Hawk caught them both. If you try to hurt others, you may get hurt yourself.
A Fox ate him. Be happy with the place you belong.

lessons.title: Lesson 32: The Serpent and the Eagle, The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing, The Bull and the Goat
steps: Read aloud: The Serpent and the Eagle, The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing, The Bull and the Goat
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing" and underline the most important word
Act out one fable with toys or puppets
questions: How did the Eagle repay the man who saved him?
Why was the Wolf in sheep's clothing caught?
Why didn't the Bull fight the rude Goat?
answers: He knocked away the poisoned horn. A kindness will come back to you.
The Shepherd chose him for dinner. Tricks can get the trickster hurt.
He was hiding from the Lion. It's wrong to pick on someone when they are in trouble.

lessons.title: Lesson 33: The Eagle and the Beetle, The Old Lion and the Fox, The Man and the Lion
steps: Read aloud: The Eagle and the Beetle, The Old Lion and the Fox, The Man and the Lion
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Man and the Lion" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today

links.label: Read “The Old Lion and the Fox”

questions: How did the Beetle get back at the Eagle?
Why didn't the Fox go into the Lion's cave?
Why did the Man and Lion disagree about the statue?
answers: She kept rolling the Eagle's eggs out of the nest. Even the smallest can stand up to a wrong.
Footprints went in but none came out. Learn from what happened to others.
A man made it, so the man won. It depends on who tells the story.

lessons.title: Lesson 34: The Ass and the Lap Dog, The Milkmaid and Her Pail, The Wolf and the Shepherd
steps: Read aloud: The Ass and the Lap Dog, The Milkmaid and Her Pail, The Wolf and the Shepherd
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Ass and the Lap Dog" in your best handwriting
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life

links.label: Read “The Ass and the Lap Dog”

questions: What happened when the Ass jumped on his master like the Lap Dog?
What made the Milkmaid spill her milk?
What did the Wolf notice about the Shepherd's dinner?
answers: He got beaten. Don't act like someone you're not just to be liked.
She was daydreaming and tossed her head. Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
They ate a lamb but would chase him for doing the same. People often blame others for things they do themselves.

lessons.title: Lesson 35: The Goatherd and the Goat, The Miser, The Wolf and the House Dog
steps: Read aloud: The Goatherd and the Goat, The Miser, The Wolf and the House Dog
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Miser" from dictation, then check it against the book

links.label: Read “The Wolf and the House Dog”

questions: Why couldn't the Goatherd hide what he did?
Why was the stone as good as the Miser's gold?
Why did the Wolf not want to be a house dog?
answers: The Goat's broken horn would show it. Bad things you do will come out.
He never used the gold. Things are only worth what you use them for.
Dogs wear a collar and chain. Being free is worth more than food.

lessons.title: Lesson 36: The Fox and the Hedgehog, The Bat and the Weasels, The Quack Toad
steps: Read aloud: The Fox and the Hedgehog, The Bat and the Weasels, The Quack Toad
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Quack Toad" and underline the most important word
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening
questions: Why didn't the Fox want the flies chased away?
How did the Bat escape both Weasels?
Why didn't the Fox believe the Toad was a doctor?
answers: Hungrier ones would come. Sometimes it's better to bear a small problem than risk a bigger one.
He said he was a mouse to one and a bird to the other. Change your plan to fit what's happening.
The Toad couldn't fix his own skin. Fix yourself before trying to fix others.

lessons.title: Lesson 37: The Fox Without a Tail, The Mischievous Dog, The Rose and the Butterfly
steps: Read aloud: The Fox Without a Tail, The Mischievous Dog, The Rose and the Butterfly
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Fox Without a Tail" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Act out one fable with toys or puppets
questions: Why did the Fox without a tail want the others to cut theirs off?
Was the Dog's clog something to be proud of?
Why couldn't the Butterfly blame the Rose?
answers: So he wouldn't look silly. Don't listen to someone who wants you to lose what you have.
No, it showed he was bad. Being known for bad things isn't being famous.
He flitted to other flowers too. Don't expect others to be loyal if you aren't.

lessons.title: Lesson 38: The Cat and the Fox, The Boy and the Nettle, The Old Lion
steps: Read aloud: The Cat and the Fox, The Boy and the Nettle, The Old Lion
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Boy and the Nettle" in your best handwriting
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today
questions: What saved the Cat when the dogs came?
How should the Boy touch a nettle next time?
How did the animals treat the Lion when he was old and weak?
answers: Her one trick of climbing a tree. Plain good sense beats lots of clever tricks.
Grab it firmly. Whatever you do, do it with all your might.
They attacked him. It's cowardly to pick on someone who can't fight back.

lessons.title: Lesson 39: The Fox and the Pheasants, Two Travelers and a Bear, The Porcupine and the Snakes
steps: Read aloud: The Fox and the Pheasants, Two Travelers and a Bear, The Porcupine and the Snakes
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Porcupine and the Snakes" from dictation, then check it against the book
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life
questions: Why did the Pheasants fall to the Fox?
What did the Bear "whisper" to the man on the ground?
What did the Porcupine do once the Snakes let him in?
answers: They watched him so hard they got dizzy. Worrying too much about danger can make you fall into it.
Don't travel with a friend who leaves you in danger. Hard times show who your true friends are.
He pushed them out with his quills. If you give a little, someone may take a lot.

lessons.title: Lesson 40: The Fox and the Monkey, The Mother and the Wolf, The Flies and the Honey
steps: Read aloud: The Fox and the Monkey, The Mother and the Wolf, The Flies and the Honey
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Fox and the Monkey" and underline the most important word
questions: Why wasn't the Monkey a good king?
Why didn't the Wolf get the child?
Why did the flies die?
answers: He fell for the Fox's trap. A real leader proves it by being wise.
The Mother didn't mean what she said. Don't believe everything you hear.
They got stuck in the honey. Being greedy for a treat can hurt you.

lessons.title: Lesson 41: The Eagle and the Kite, The Stag, the Sheep, and the Wolf, The Animals and the Plague
steps: Read aloud: The Eagle and the Kite, The Stag, the Sheep, and the Wolf, The Animals and the Plague
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Stag, the Sheep, and the Wolf" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening

links.label: Read “The Stag, the Sheep, and the Wolf”

questions: Why did the Kite say he could catch an Ostrich?
Why wouldn't the Sheep lend wheat to the Stag?
Who was blamed for the plague?
answers: He wanted the Eagle to marry him. People will say anything to win what they want.
She didn't trust him or his friend the Wolf. Two untrustworthy people don't make one you can trust.
The Ass, who did the smallest wrong. Sometimes the weak are punished for what the strong did.

lessons.title: Lesson 42: The Shepherd and the Lion, The Dog and His Reflection, The Hare and the Tortoise
steps: Read aloud: The Shepherd and the Lion, The Dog and His Reflection, The Hare and the Tortoise
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Hare and the Tortoise" in your best handwriting
Act out one fable with toys or puppets
questions: What did the Shepherd do when he really saw the Lion?
Why did the Dog lose his bone?
Who won the race?
answers: He ran and wished it gone. Be careful what you wish for.
He snapped at his reflection. Being greedy is foolish.
The Tortoise, by never stopping. Slow and steady wins the race.

lessons.title: Lesson 43: The Bees and Wasps, and the Hornet, The Lark and Her Young Ones, The Cat and the Old Rat
steps: Read aloud: The Bees and Wasps, and the Hornet, The Lark and Her Young Ones, The Cat and the Old Rat
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Bees and Wasps, and the Hornet" from dictation, then check it against the book
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today

links.label: Read “The Bees and Wasps, and the Hornet”
Read “The Lark and Her Young Ones”
Read “The Cat and the Old Rat”

questions: How did the Judge know who made the honey?
When did the Lark finally move her babies?
Why didn't the old Rat go near the flour-covered lump?
answers: The Wasps couldn't make comb. What you can really do proves who you are.
When the Farmer said he'd cut the wheat himself. Doing it yourself is the best help.
He'd been tricked by the Cat before. A wise one doesn't get tricked twice.

lessons.title: Lesson 44: The Fox and the Crow, The Ass and Its Shadow, The Miller, His Son, and the Ass
steps: Read aloud: The Fox and the Crow, The Ass and Its Shadow, The Miller, His Son, and the Ass
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Ass and Its Shadow" and underline the most important word
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life

links.label: Read “The Miller, His Son, and the Ass”

questions: How did the Fox get the Crow's cheese?
What happened while the men fought over the shadow?
Why did the Miller lose his Ass?
answers: He praised her voice so she sang. A flatterer gets things from people who listen.
The Ass ran away. If you fight over little things, you can lose what matters.
He tried to do what everyone said. If you try to please everyone, you please no one.

lessons.title: Lesson 45: The Ant and the Dove, The Man and the Satyr, The Wolf, the Kid, and the Goat
steps: Read aloud: The Ant and the Dove, The Man and the Satyr, The Wolf, the Kid, and the Goat
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Wolf, the Kid, and the Goat" (younger children can trace it after you write it)

links.label: Read “The Wolf, the Kid, and the Goat”

questions: How did the Ant save the Dove?
Why did the Satyr leave the Man?
Why didn't the Kid open the door to the Wolf?
answers: She bit the hunter so he missed. A kindness is never wasted.
He blew hot and cold. Don't trust someone who says one thing and then the opposite.
He asked for the password and to see a white paw. It's good to be extra careful.

lessons.title: Lesson 46: The Swallow and the Crow, Jupiter and the Monkey, The Lion, the Ass, and the Fox
steps: Read aloud: The Swallow and the Crow, Jupiter and the Monkey, The Lion, the Ass, and the Fox
Pause after each fable and ask your child to narrate it
Copy the moral of "The Swallow and the Crow" in your best handwriting
Look at Milo Winter's picture for one fable and tell what is happening

links.label: Read “The Lion, the Ass, and the Fox”

questions: When did the Crow say the Swallow wasn't a good friend?
Why did Mother Monkey love her baby most?
How did the Fox learn to share with the Lion?
answers: In winter when the Swallow left. A friend only in good times isn't much of a friend.
Mothers love their babies no matter what. Mother love is blind.
He saw what happened to the Ass. Learn from other people's mistakes.

lessons.title: Lesson 47: The Lion's Share, The Mole and His Mother, The North Wind and the Sun
steps: Read aloud: The Lion's Share, The Mole and His Mother, The North Wind and the Sun
Your child narrates each fable back, then you talk about the moral together
Write the moral of "The Mole and His Mother" from dictation, then check it against the book
Act out one fable with toys or puppets

links.label: Read “The North Wind and the Sun”

questions: Why did the Lion keep all the meat?
How did the Mother Mole show her son he couldn't smell?
How did the Sun get the traveler to take off his cloak?
answers: He was the strongest. Sometimes bullies take everything, and that isn't fair.
She held up something and he guessed wrong. If you brag, others will find what you can't do.
By shining warmly. Being gentle and kind works better than being rough.

lessons.title: Lesson 48: The Hare and His Ears, The Wolves and the Sheep, The Cock and the Fox
steps: Read aloud: The Hare and His Ears, The Wolves and the Sheep, The Cock and the Fox
Ask your child to retell their favorite of the three to someone else at home
Copy the moral of "The Cock and the Fox" and underline the most important word
Draw a picture of your favorite fable from today
questions: Why did the Hare run away from the Lion's kingdom?
What happened when the Sheep sent the Dogs away?
Why didn't the Cock help the trapped Fox?
answers: He was afraid his ears would be called horns. A bully will find any excuse to pick on you.
The Wolves ate them. Don't give up your true friends for your enemies.
He knew the Fox would eat the hens. Don't help someone who will do harm.

lessons.title: Lesson 49: The Ass in the Lion's Skin, The Fisherman and the Little Fish, The Fighting Cocks and the Eagle
steps: Read aloud: The Ass in the Lion's Skin, The Fisherman and the Little Fish, The Fighting Cocks and the Eagle
After each fable, have your child tell it back in their own words
Copy the moral of "The Ass in the Lion's Skin" (younger children can trace it after you write it)
Talk about a time you saw this lesson happen in real life

links.label: Read “The Ass in the Lion's Skin”
Read “The Fisherman and the Little Fish”
Read “The Fighting Cocks and the Eagle”

questions: How did the Fox know the "Lion" was an Ass?
Why did the Fisherman keep the little fish?
What happened to the proud Cock who crowed on the wall?
answers: He heard it bray. You can dress up, but your words show who you are.
A small fish now is better than a big one later. A sure small thing is better than a big promise.
An Eagle carried him off. Pride comes before a fall.
